title: How To Make Your Students Smarter
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues that many students underperform because they've internalized a belief that they're simply incapable, a self-image reinforced when teachers over-help, repeat themselves, and dumb down material, however well-intentioned. He grounds this in historical research, citing 1920s psychologist Prescott Lecky's findings linking poor grades to self-concept, and the later Rosenthal effect showing teacher expectations dramatically shape student performance. The article offers a concrete list of behaviors meant to signal belief in students' capability: being reluctant to help after a lesson, extending independent work time, refusing to micromanage, and raising standards while assuming students can handle them. He rejects the framing of students as victims needing rescue as a 'lie,' arguing that barring intellectual disability, all students can succeed given genuine belief and high expectations from their teacher. The piece closes by asserting that shifting a teacher's own perception of students, from fragile to capable, can transform a class within a single school year.
points: Students who believe they're incapable enter a reinforcing cycle of low effort and more failure, a cycle worsened when teachers over-help or dumb down material.
Historical research cited includes 1920s psychologist Prescott Lecky's findings linking poor grades to self-concept, and the later Rosenthal effect on teacher expectations.
Concrete behaviors recommended to build student capability include being reluctant to help after a lesson, extending independent work time, and refusing to micromanage.
The framing of students as victims needing rescue is explicitly rejected; barring intellectual disability, all students are described as capable of succeeding.
A teacher's shift from seeing students as fragile to seeing them as capable is framed as powerful enough to transform a class within one school year.
quotes: Many students do poorly because they believe they’re incapable.
This isn’t a new phenomenon. In the 1920s, psychologist and teacher Prescott Lecky conducted extensive research into academic success and self-image.

His conclusions have been repeated many times over, most notably by researcher Robert Rosenthal. Now called the Rosenthal effect, it proves that the expectations of the teacher have a dramatic affect on the performance of students.
Say often, “You don’t need me.” “You can do this.” “I believe in you.

Unless a student has an intellectual disability, there is no reason for them not to succeed in school. Yes, they have mountains to climb. Some have trauma and tough home lives. Yes, yes, and yes. Agreed.

If you can make the switch from believing they’re at the mercy of circumstance to smart, capable people who have the power to succeed just as they are , despite it all, their lives will be transformed in nine months.
